name: count the repeat that made the page stand up
one_line: A block of letters whose repeat shortens from left to right, so that two eyes together see four steps and one eye sees a texture.
how: Print thirteen rows of forty-four lowercase letters in a fixed-pitch face at ten characters to the inch. Let the pattern repeat every fourteen characters on the left and shorten to thirteen, twelve and eleven going right: four steps, each nearer than the last. Print how to look — page against the nose, too close to focus, then moved away slowly without trying to focus — and that a minute is enough, because aiming the eyes far while focusing near is tiring on purpose. Print that between one person in twenty and one in three cannot see it, and that this is how their eyes are. Then ask, in pencil on the flat page, how long the repeat is in each of the four steps.

knobs.knob: whether the closing question is done flat or in relief
knobs.effect: counted with a pencil on the flat page, it can be answered by everybody including whoever cannot fuse the image, and it comes back on the sheet; asked about what they saw in relief, it excludes a fifth of readers and returns nothing.

at ten characters to the inch, fourteen characters is 35.6 mm, under the 63 mm between most people's eyes; set the type larger and the repeat passes 63 mm, nobody can fuse it, and nothing on the page says why.
repeats of 14, 13, 12 and 11 give four distinct planes and four numbers to count; two planes are as easy to see, give one flat step, and leave the closing question almost nothing to ask.

the same block read the two ways gives the depth the opposite way round, so a page that says which way to look describes one of two effects; saying nothing lets two readers see opposite staircases and both be right.

where_the_work_is: In the repeat length, the only parameter and measured in characters. Everything else — which letters, how many rows — can be anything, and the four numbers that come back are the four repeats chosen before printing.
breaks: A proportional face destroys it completely: the repeat stops being a constant width, nothing fuses, and no sign on the page says anything is wrong. It has to be fixed-pitch. The print scale matters in one direction — larger type pushes the repeat past the 63 mm between the eyes and kills it, smaller type is safe. Between 5% and 30% of readers cannot see the relief on any page, which is why the question asked is done flat with a pencil. On the display the forty-four columns fit; whether the repeat lands under 63 mm depends on the panel's width, which has not been measured.
